911.title: Titus Brandsma (1881–1942)
911.hook: a Dutch Carmelite who carried a letter from editor to editor, telling Catholic papers to refuse Nazi propaganda
911.howItsDone: Catholics honor St. Titus Brandsma as a martyr, and Catholic journalists' groups name him as a patron and example; Carmelites keep his feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Franz Jägerstätter, the farmer and sacristan who would not fight. Your line was one farmer said no. What small no did you say? Today, a priest who said no with a newspaper. Day nine hundred eleven.

A train compartment in the occupied Netherlands. A small, thin priest in a Carmelite habit, glasses, a briefcase on his knees. Inside the briefcase is a letter from the Dutch bishops. He gets off in one town, finds the office of the local Catholic newspaper, sits down with the editor, and explains the letter. Then back to the station, and the next town, and the next editor. He knows the occupiers will hear about this. Titus Brandsma, friar, professor and newspaperman, keeps going anyway.
screen: `A PRIEST WITH A BRIEFCASE.` → `EDITOR AFTER EDITOR.` → `HE KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the professor. Titus was a Carmelite friar and a scholar of mysticism, a teacher at the Catholic university in Nijmegen. He also loved newspapers. He wrote for them, edited, and served as spiritual adviser to the Catholic journalists of his country. Second, the order. Under the occupation, the Nazi authorities demanded that Catholic papers print their propaganda, including notices for the Dutch Nazi party. The bishops said no: a Catholic paper that printed it could no longer call itself Catholic. Somebody had to carry that message to the editors, face to face, so no one could say they hadn't heard. Titus said he would go. Third, the cost. He was arrested and questioned. Asked why he resisted, he said, in substance, that the Nazi ideas could not be squared with the Gospel. He was sent from prison to prison, then to Dachau. Weak and sick, he was taken to the camp hospital and killed with an injection. Tradition says he gave his rosary to the nurse who did it. Fourth, the truth. Jesus says in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." Set beside his life, it reads like a rule for newsrooms too: telling the truth includes refusing to print a lie, even a paid one.
screen: `A PROFESSOR WHO LOVED NEWSPAPERS.` · `NO NAZI PROPAGANDA IN OUR PAPERS.` · `ARRESTED, THEN DACHAU.` · `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.` · then, large: `KNOW THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell the truth in public. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you speak to more than one person: a team chat, a family thread, a meeting, a post. Is there something true that needs saying there, plainly and kindly? Or something false you've been letting pass, that you could quietly correct? Choose one sentence. Say it to yourself first, slowly, until it's clear and fair. If you pray, you can ask for Titus's steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Titus Brandsma. A Dutch Carmelite and journalist who carried the bishops' refusal of Nazi propaganda to editor after editor, and died at Dachau.
Your line: a journalist's courage. Today, say that one true sentence in public, or correct one thing that isn't true. Day nine hundred eleven.

912.title: Irena Sendler
912.hook: a Polish Catholic social worker helps smuggle Jewish children out of the Warsaw Ghetto, and buries their names
912.howItsDone: Catholic schools in Poland and elsewhere teach Irena Sendler's story, and Jewish and Catholic groups honor her together as one of the Righteous Among the Nations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Titus Brandsma, carrying the bishops' letter from editor to editor. Your line was a journalist's courage. Did you say your true sentence? Today, a rescuer with a pass and a list. Day nine hundred twelve.

Slips of tissue paper, each with a child's name on it. The real name, the name they were born with, and next to it the new name they now answer to, and where they've been taken. The slips go into glass jars, and the jars go into the ground under an apple tree in a friend's yard in Warsaw. That's the story usually told about Irena Sendler, a Catholic social worker. She buried the names so that one day, when the war was over, someone could dig them up and give the children back their families.
screen: `NAMES ON TISSUE PAPER.` → `JARS UNDER AN APPLE TREE.` → `TO GIVE THE CHILDREN BACK.`

segments.voice: It began with a pass. Irena worked in Warsaw's welfare office. When the Nazis walled the city's Jews into the Ghetto, disease spread inside, and she was able to get a pass to go in as part of the health inspections. Inside, she saw children starving. Second, the network. She was not alone. She worked with a secret Polish group that helped Jews, known by a code name, Żegota, and with others, Catholic and Jewish, inside and outside the walls. Children were carried out in ambulances, in boxes and sacks, through buildings with doors on both sides. Then they needed new names, papers and homes: Polish families, orphanages, convents where sisters took them in. Third, the parents. The hardest moment, by her own later account, was asking Jewish mothers and fathers to hand their children to a stranger, with no promise of anything. Some said yes. Some could not. Fourth, the arrest. The Gestapo arrested her and beat her badly, and she was sentenced to death. Żegota bribed a guard, and she got away and went on working under another name. She never gave up the list. Jesus says in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he that shall receive one such little child in my name, receiveth me." After the war, Israel's Holocaust memorial, Yad Vashem, honored her as Righteous Among the Nations, and in later life she said she had not done enough.
screen: `A PASS INTO THE GHETTO.` · `ŻEGOTA AND THE NETWORK.` · `PARENTS HANDING OVER CHILDREN.` · `ARRESTED, AND STILL THE LIST.` · then, large: `RECEIVE ONE SUCH LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a rescuer. Settle, and breathe. Hold Irena in mind, and then the people she worked with whose names are less known: the drivers, the sisters, the families who said yes to a child at the door. Let them be real people, with their own fears and their own doors. Then think of someone in your own life who stepped in for someone else when it cost them. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, simply say their name to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Irena Sendler. A Polish Catholic social worker who helped smuggle Jewish children out of the Warsaw Ghetto, and kept their real names hidden in jars.
Your line: she hid the names. Today, learn the name of one rescuer, from your family, your town or history, and say it to someone else. Day nine hundred twelve.

913.title: Dorothy Day (1897–1980)
913.hook: a journalist starts a newspaper and opens houses of hospitality in New York
913.howItsDone: Catholic Worker houses of hospitality still serve meals and offer beds in cities and on farms, run by volunteers who live simply and publish their own papers; Dorothy Day's cause for canonization is open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irena Sendler and the jars of names under an apple tree. Your line was she hid the names. Whose name did you learn? Today, back across the ocean, to a soup line in New York. Day nine hundred thirteen.

Union Square, New York, in the hard years of the Depression. Street speakers on boxes, men out of work, pamphlets everywhere. A woman is selling a brand-new newspaper, cheap, with a plain title: The Catholic Worker. She has written for radical papers for years. She has marched, been arrested, loved and lost, and become a Catholic, to the surprise of her old friends. Now Dorothy Day wants a paper that tells workers the Church cares about them, and she is out in the square, selling it.
screen: `A NEW PAPER IN UNION SQUARE.` → `A RADICAL WHO BECAME CATHOLIC.` → `DOROTHY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the convert. Dorothy was a journalist and a socialist who knew the poor from the inside, from rented rooms and picket lines. When her daughter Tamar was born, she was overwhelmed with gratitude, and she had the baby baptized, and then was baptized herself. It cost her the man she loved, who wanted no part of religion. She wrote about that grief openly. Second, the paper. With a French wanderer named Peter Maurin, who is tomorrow's story, she started The Catholic Worker. It took the Church's teaching on workers and the poor and put it on the street, in plain language. Third, the house. People read the paper and came to the door hungry. So she opened a house of hospitality: soup, coffee, a bed, a seat at the table, with no forms to fill in. Then another house, in other cities, and farms. They called the whole movement by the paper's name, the Catholic Worker. The prophet Isaiah says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Deal thy bread to the hungry, and bring the needy and the harbourless into thy house." Dorothy took it literally, day after day. Fourth, the title. She wrote the story of her life and called it The Long Loneliness. Her closing thought, in paraphrase: the answer to that loneliness is love, and love comes with community. Today the Church calls her a Servant of God, the first step toward sainthood. She was wary of being called a saint, saying it made her too easy to dismiss.
screen: `A RADICAL BAPTIZED.` · `A PAPER FOR WORKERS.` · `A HOUSE WITH NO FORMS.` · `THE LONG LONELINESS.` · then, large: `DEAL THY BREAD TO THE HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone today. Settle, and breathe. Picture a table, any table, yours or a soup kitchen's or a desk at work. Now let one person come to mind who could use something to eat: a neighbor who lives alone, a coworker who skips lunch, someone you pass on the street, a food bank that's running low. Decide on one meal, one sandwich, one bag of groceries, one coffee. If you pray, you can pray for that person as you plan. The bell holds the time.
Catholic Worker. Dorothy Day's newspaper, and the movement of houses of hospitality that grew from it, feeding and housing whoever came to the door.
Your line: the long loneliness. Today, feed one person, and if you can, sit down and eat with them. Day nine hundred thirteen.

914.title: Peter Maurin
914.hook: the French wandering teacher who gave Dorothy Day her plan
914.howItsDone: Catholic Worker communities still hold round-table discussions for clarification of thought, and some still read Peter Maurin's easy essays aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dorothy Day and the Catholic Worker: a paper, a soup pot, a house with no forms. Your line was the long loneliness. Who did you feed? Today, the man who was waiting at her door with a plan. Day nine hundred fourteen.

A knock at a New York apartment door. Dorothy Day comes home and finds a shabby, broad-shouldered Frenchman with a thick accent waiting for her, already talking. His suit looks slept in. His pockets are full of papers. He has heard she wants to do something for the poor, and he has a plan. He keeps coming back, day after day, talking about saints, history, farms and the Gospel, until she is convinced. Peter Maurin has found his listener.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `A FRENCHMAN WITH A PLAN.` → `HE KEEPS COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Peter started as a wanderer. He grew up in a farming family in France. He came to North America and drifted through hard work: laborer, homesteader, handyman, teacher of French. He owned almost nothing and seemed to want it that way. He read widely, and he lived what he read. Second, the essays. He wrote his ideas in short lines, broken up like poems, so they could be read aloud on a street corner. He called them easy essays. They were easy to say, and hard to live. Their spirit, in paraphrase: build a society where it's easier for people to be good. Third, the plan. He gave Dorothy three pieces. Round-table discussions, where workers and scholars would sit together and think things through; he called it clarification of thought. Houses of hospitality, where the hungry would be fed as guests, not cases. And farming communes, where people could work the land together. The paper became the way to spread it. Fourth, the root. Peter pointed back to the first Christians. Acts says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And all they that believed, were together, and had all things common." He didn't think that was only a story. He thought it was a plan anyone could start, at their own table. He spent his last years ill and forgetful, living at a Catholic Worker farm, cared for by the movement he helped begin. Dorothy kept saying the vision was his.
screen: `A WANDERER WHO OWNED NOTHING.` · `EASY TO SAY, HARD TO LIVE.` · `TALK, HOUSES, FARMS.` · `ALL THINGS COMMON.` · then, large: `CLARIFICATION OF THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share an idea with someone. Settle, and breathe. Peter's way was simple: say a good idea out loud to whoever would listen. Find one idea that has helped you lately, from a book, a homily, a friend, this path. Put it into one short line, easy to say. Say it to yourself a few times until it sounds like you. Then think of who might need to hear it today. If you pray, you can pray for that person. The bell holds the time.
Peter Maurin. A French wanderer and teacher who gave Dorothy Day the Catholic Worker's plan: talk, houses of hospitality, and farms.
Your line: easy essays. Today, share your one short line with one person, out loud, and let them answer. Day nine hundred fourteen.

915.title: Gianna Beretta Molla (1922–1962)
915.hook: an Italian doctor, wife and mother, honored by the Church as a saint
915.howItsDone: Catholics ask St. Gianna Beretta Molla to pray for mothers, families, doctors and the unborn, and some Catholic hospitals and pregnancy centers bear her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Maurin, the wanderer with a plan and a pocket full of short lines. Your line was easy essays. Who heard your idea? Today, a saint with a stethoscope. Day nine hundred fifteen.

A small-town clinic in northern Italy. The doctor on duty is a young woman, seeing mothers, babies and old people, and making house calls when they can't come in. In her free time she skis, climbs, goes to concerts, and paints. She is married to an engineer named Pietro, and they have young children at home. She writes him warm, ordinary letters about meals, trips and the children. Gianna Beretta Molla looks nothing like the saints in old paintings.
screen: `A DOCTOR ON HOUSE CALLS.` → `SKIS, PAINTS, WRITES LETTERS.` → `GIANNA BERETTA MOLLA.`

segments.voice: First, the calling. Gianna trained as a doctor and cared especially for mothers and children. She saw medicine as a way of serving Christ in the sick, and she was active in her parish youth work. Second, the marriage. She thought long about whether to become a missionary or to marry. She married Pietro, and her letters to him are full of joy in plain, everyday things. Third, the choice. During another pregnancy, her doctors found a growth on her womb. There were choices to make. She chose the operation that would remove the growth and protect the pregnancy, knowing it carried more risk for her. Later, she told those around her that if a choice had to be made between her life and the baby's, they should save the baby. Her daughter was born healthy. Gianna died a few days later. Fourth, the saint. The Church has canonized her, and Pietro and their children lived to see it. Catholics honor her choice as a gift freely given, not a rule laid on every mother. Jesus says in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Her letters keep the ordinary days in view as well: a doctor and a mother, at work and at home.
screen: `MEDICINE AS SERVICE.` · `A MARRIAGE OF PLAIN JOYS.` · `SAVE THE BABY.` · `A GIFT, NOT A RULE.` · then, large: `GREATER LOVE THAN THIS NO MAN HATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for mothers who are ill, or hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Let one mother come to mind who is sick right now: your own, a friend, a neighbor, a woman in a hospital you'll never meet. Think of her children, her worries, the doctors and nurses around her. Breathe slowly, as if you were sitting by her bed. If you pray, you can ask Gianna to pray with you for her. If you don't, simply wish her strength and rest. The bell holds the time.
Gianna Beretta Molla. An Italian doctor, wife and mother who protected her unborn daughter at the cost of her own life, and whom the Church honors as a saint.
Your line: a doctor and a mother. Today, check on one mother who is unwell, or thank one doctor or nurse who cared for someone you love. Day nine hundred fifteen.

916.title: Pier Giorgio Frassati (1901–1925)
916.hook: a mountain-climbing student who quietly served Turin's poor
916.howItsDone: Some young Catholics name Pier Giorgio Frassati as a patron, and Catholic youth groups and campus ministries organize hikes and climbs in his memory, sometimes under his phrase verso l'alto.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gianna Beretta Molla, who skied and painted and made house calls. Your line was a doctor and a mother. Who did you check on? Today, another saint who loved the mountains. Day nine hundred sixteen.

A funeral in Turin, and the family is confused. The young man in the coffin was the son of a rich and well-known household. They expected the city's important people. They did not expect the streets to fill with the poor: widows, old men, families from the back alleys, people the family had never seen. They had come, one after another, to say that this young man had brought them food, coal, medicine and rent money, quietly, for years. His family hadn't known. That is how the Frassatis learned who their son, Pier Giorgio, had been.
screen: `A FUNERAL IN TURIN.` → `THE POOR FILL THE STREETS.` → `HIS FAMILY HADN'T KNOWN.`

segments.voice: The mountains come first. Pier Giorgio loved the mountains. He hiked and climbed with friends in the Alps, laughing, singing, playing pranks. On one photo of himself on a climb he wrote a short Italian phrase: verso l'alto, to the heights. Second, the student. He studied engineering, and tradition says he chose mining so he could work beside miners, among the hardest-working poor he knew. He went to daily Mass, prayed the rosary, and threw himself into Catholic student groups and politics. Third, the hidden work. Through the Saint Vincent de Paul Society he visited the poor in their homes, week after week. He gave away his money, his coat, his tram fare, and then ran home to be on time for dinner. He didn't tell his parents. Fourth, the end. He fell ill suddenly with polio and died within days, still a young man. Tradition says he caught it from the sick he visited. Even in his last hours, he sent a note asking a friend to bring medicine to a poor man he could no longer reach. The Psalm says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me." For Pier Giorgio, those who knew him said, climbing was a way of praying. And back in the city there were other climbs: the stairs up to the rooms of the poor. The Church has now canonized him. To the heights meant both: the peak, and the poor man's attic.
screen: `VERSO L'ALTO.` · `A STUDENT WHO CHOSE THE MINES.` · `HIDDEN WORK, WEEK AFTER WEEK.` · `A NOTE FROM HIS DEATHBED.` · then, large: `I HAVE LIFTED UP MY EYES TO THE MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go climb something. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture the climb that's within your reach today: a hill, a trail, a park, a flight of stairs at work. Feel your legs ready for it. Now add Pier Giorgio's second half: who is at the top of a staircase near you, someone you could visit or bring something to? Hold both, the climb and the person. If you pray, you can lift your eyes, the way the psalm does. The bell holds the time.
Pier Giorgio Frassati. A young man from Turin who climbed mountains, studied engineering, and quietly served the poor, honored by the Church as a saint.
Your line: to the heights. Today, climb something, even a staircase, and on the way, do one quiet good thing nobody will hear about. Day nine hundred sixteen.

917.title: Good Pope John (1958–1963)
917.hook: a farmer's son, warm and brave, whose letter on peace was addressed to all people of goodwill
917.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint John XXIII on his feast day, and Pacem in Terris is still read in Catholic schools, parishes and peace groups as a foundation of the Church's teaching on peace and human rights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pier Giorgio Frassati, the student who climbed mountains and quietly visited the poor. Your line was to the heights. What did you climb, a hill or a staircase? Today, a pope the people of Rome simply called good. Day nine hundred seventeen.

A letter from a pope usually opens by saying who it is for. The bishops. The clergy. The faithful. This one does all that, and then it keeps going. It is addressed, its opening says, to all men of good will. Not only Catholics. Not only believers. Anyone who means well, wherever they are. The man who signed it had grown up in a farming family in the hills of northern Italy, and he never lost the manner of a country priest: jokes, plain talk, a big laugh. People in Rome gave him a plainer name. Good Pope John.
screen: `A LETTER WITH A WIDE ADDRESS.` → `A FARMING FAMILY.` → `GOOD POPE JOHN.`

segments.voice: His name was Angelo Roncalli, and as pope he took the name John. Four things about him. First, the farm. He came from a family that worked the land, and he wrote about that childhood with affection in his spiritual diary, later published as Journal of a Soul. He did not pretend to be grander than he was. Second, the window. He surprised the Church by calling a council, a gathering of the world's bishops in Rome, which became the Second Vatican Council. Tradition says he described it as opening a window to let in fresh air. What that council changed in ordinary parishes is tomorrow's story. Third, the letter. As pope he wrote an encyclical called Pacem in Terris, Latin for peace on earth. It says that peace among nations has to stand on four things: truth, justice, love and freedom. It speaks of the rights every human being has simply by being human, and the duties that come with them. And it was addressed not only to Catholics but to all people of good will. Fourth, the echo. That phrase has an old sound for Catholics. On the night of Christ's birth, Luke's Gospel says, the angels sang, in the Douay-Rheims, "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." A pope borrowing the angels' address for a letter about peace. It was his way of saying that the work of peace is shared with anyone willing to do it.
screen: `A FARMER'S SON NAMED ANGELO.` · `HE OPENS A WINDOW: A COUNCIL.` · `PEACE ON TRUTH, JUSTICE, LOVE, FREEDOM.` · `THE ANGELS' ADDRESS, BORROWED.` · then, large: `ON EARTH PEACE TO MEN OF GOOD WILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write, in your head first, to someone of goodwill. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who means well, maybe someone you disagree with about a lot, but whose good intentions you trust. A neighbor, a coworker, a relative across a political line. Let one honest sentence form: thank you for something, or I see what you're trying to do. Keep it short and true. If you pray, you can pray the angels' line from Luke for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind and wish them well. After the bell, send it. The bell holds the time.
Good Pope John. Angelo Roncalli, a farmer's son who became pope, called a council and wrote Pacem in Terris to all people of good will.

Your line: all people of goodwill. This week ran from Titus Brandsma and Irena Sendler through Dorothy Day, Peter Maurin, Gianna Beretta Molla and Pier Giorgio Frassati, to Good Pope John. Today, send that one message. Day nine hundred seventeen.

fork.setup: you're Pope John, writing a letter about peace in a tense world. who do you address it to?
options: the bishops only.
Catholics everywhere.
all people of good will.
fork.reveal: after the bishops and the faithful, he added all people of good will, borrowing the angels' address from Luke.

original.note: Latin: peace on earth, the opening words that give the encyclical its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pope's letter is written for Catholics only.
what it means: Pacem in Terris was addressed to all people of good will, believers or not.
what a scholar hears: the Latin address, men of good will, uses the angels' words from Luke 2:14 in the Vulgate.
